summary: LLM inference costs are dominated by token volume, and most production workloads contain far more repetition and waste than teams expect. Layering caching (exact-match, prefix, and semantic), prompt compression, model routing, and output constraints commonly cuts API spend by 40-80% while improving time-to-first-token by 13-31%. The highest-ROI approach is combining multiple techniques: no single method wins, but stacked optimizations compound.

techniques.name: Provider prefix / prompt caching (exact-match)
techniques.description: Reuses the cached KV state for a repeated prompt prefix (e.g. a long system prompt or shared context) so the model skips recomputing the prefill stage for that portion. It still performs normal decoding, so it reduces input-token cost and latency but not output cost.
techniques.savings: 41-80% cost reduction on cached input; 13-31% faster time-to-first-token
techniques.example: Place your large static system prompt and few-shot examples at the very start of every request so OpenAI/Anthropic can cache the shared prefix across calls, charging reduced rates for the repeated tokens.

techniques.name: Semantic caching
techniques.description: Matches incoming queries by meaning rather than exact text using embedding similarity, and returns a previously generated response without calling the model at all. Unlike prefix caching it saves both input AND output tokens, and can bypass inference entirely on near-matches.
techniques.savings: ~45% cache hit rate; up to 100% savings on each hit (no inference call)
techniques.example: Embed each incoming query, search cached embeddings with cosine similarity > 0.85, and if 'How do I return a product?' matches a cached 'What's your return policy?' response, return it instantly instead of calling the LLM.

techniques.name: Multi-tier caching strategy
techniques.description: Layers exact-match caching (sub-millisecond for identical queries), semantic caching (slightly higher latency for similar queries), and session context management together. Each layer catches a different class of repetition, and instrumenting hit rate per layer reveals where the real savings are.
techniques.savings: Substantial — combined layers often cut token consumption dramatically in high-repetition chatbots
techniques.example: Check an exact-match cache first, fall back to a semantic cache on a miss, and only call the LLM if both miss — using Redis to back all layers.

techniques.name: Prompt compression
techniques.description: Reduces the number of input tokens by removing redundancy, trimming boilerplate, summarizing context, or using compression models (e.g. LLMLingua) to compress prompts while preserving meaning.
techniques.example: Run long retrieved documents through LLMLingua to compress a 2,000-token context down to ~1,400 tokens before sending it to the model.

techniques.name: Model routing (tiered models)
techniques.description: Routes each request to the cheapest model capable of handling it, sending simple queries to small/cheap models and reserving frontier models for hard tasks. A classifier or heuristic decides the tier per request.
techniques.savings: Large — e.g. routing 70% to cheap tiers, 25% to mid, 5% to frontier
techniques.example: Route 70% of traffic to GPT-3.5/4o-mini, 25% to a mid-tier model, and only 5% to GPT-4-class models for the hardest queries.

techniques.name: Output constraints
techniques.description: Limits generated output length via max_tokens caps, structured/JSON output schemas, and 'be concise' instructions. Output tokens are often priced higher than input tokens, so constraining them directly lowers cost.
techniques.example: Set max_tokens=150 and request a strict JSON schema so the model returns only the needed fields instead of verbose prose.

techniques.name: RAG / context optimization
techniques.description: Reduces token usage without changing model or architecture by retrieving fewer, higher-quality documents (reranking top-K), trimming retrieved chunks, and managing conversation context so stale turns are dropped.
techniques.example: Rerank retrieved chunks and pass only the top 3 most relevant instead of a naive top-10, cutting context tokens by more than half.

techniques.name: KV cache management (self-hosted inference)
techniques.description: At the inference-server level, techniques organized by a March 2026 Dell survey into cache eviction (dropping low-importance tokens), cache compression (quantization/pooling), hybrid memory (offloading to CPU/NVMe), and novel attention mechanisms (linear/log-linear attention). No single technique wins; combinations work best.
techniques.savings: Varies — improves memory efficiency and throughput on self-hosted deployments
techniques.example: Enable KV-cache quantization and eviction in vLLM to fit longer contexts and more concurrent requests on the same GPU.

techniques.name: Request batching
techniques.description: Groups multiple requests together for inference so fixed per-call overhead and GPU utilization are amortized, lowering effective cost per request on self-hosted or batch-API endpoints.
techniques.savings: Up to ~50% via provider batch APIs
techniques.example: Submit non-urgent embeddings or classification jobs to OpenAI's Batch API for a ~50% discount versus synchronous calls.

tools.name: GPTCache
tools.description: Open-source semantic caching library that stores LLM responses and returns cached answers for semantically similar queries using embedding similarity and a vector store.
tools.pricing_paid: Free (open source, Apache 2.0); you pay only for your own infra

tools.name: Redis / Redis LangCache (semantic cache)
tools.description: Redis powers multi-tier caching with sub-millisecond exact-match lookups and vector-based semantic caching, and offers LangCache as a managed semantic cache for LLM apps.
tools.pricing_paid: Free OSS/community tier; Redis Cloud and LangCache priced by usage/tier

tools.name: LiteLLM
tools.description: Unified proxy/SDK across 100+ LLM providers with built-in caching, model routing, fallbacks, rate limiting, and spend tracking.
tools.pricing_paid: Free open source; LiteLLM Enterprise with SSO/support via custom pricing

tools.name: Helicone
tools.description: LLM observability and gateway platform providing caching, cost/usage analytics, rate limiting, and request logging via a drop-in proxy.
tools.pricing_paid: Free tier; paid plans from ~$20/user/month plus usage-based tiers

tools.name: LangChain
tools.description: Framework for building LLM apps with built-in LLM caching (in-memory, SQLite, Redis, semantic), prompt templating, RAG, and routing utilities.
tools.pricing_paid: Free open source; LangSmith observability has free + paid plans from ~$39/user/month

tools.name: LLMLingua
tools.description: Microsoft Research prompt-compression toolkit that compresses prompts (and retrieved context) to reduce input tokens while preserving task performance.

tools.name: vCache
tools.description: Semantic cache that returns cached responses for semantically similar prompts under user-defined error-rate guarantees, saving both input and output tokens.

tools.name: OpenRouter
tools.description: Unified API gateway across many model providers enabling easy model routing, fallbacks, and price/performance comparison from a single endpoint.
tools.pricing_paid: Pay-as-you-go passthrough pricing with a small routing fee; free credits available

tools.name: vLLM
tools.description: High-throughput open-source inference server with PagedAttention, continuous batching, and KV-cache optimizations for self-hosted model serving.
tools.pricing_paid: Free (open source, Apache 2.0); you pay only for GPU/infra

quick_wins: Enable provider prompt/prefix caching by moving large static system prompts and few-shot examples to the start of every request — easy 41-80% savings on repeated input tokens.
Cap output with max_tokens and request concise/structured (JSON) responses to cut output tokens by ~50%, since output is the most expensive token type.
Add a semantic cache (GPTCache or Redis LangCache) in front of your LLM to skip inference entirely on ~45% of repeated or similar queries.
Route requests by difficulty — send the bulk of traffic to a cheap small model (4o-mini/3.5) via LiteLLM or OpenRouter and reserve frontier models for the hardest 5%.
Instrument cost and cache-hit rate per layer (e.g. with Helicone) before optimizing further, and skip optimization entirely for low-volume apps where engineering time exceeds the savings.
